h1: Hallertau Blanc hops for white wine and gooseberry notes
title: Hallertau Blanc Hops: White Wine in Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: What Hallertau Blanc hops taste like, why their white wine and gooseberry notes need late additions and the beer styles they suit.
teaser: Hallertau Blanc smells more like a glass of crisp white wine than a German hop. Here is how to keep that character.
standfirst: Hallertau Blanc is one of the German fruit hops from the Hüll breeding programme. Its aroma of white grape, gooseberry and passion fruit is unusual, delicate and easy to lose in the kettle.
sections: A German hop that does not taste German

Hallertau Blanc was released by the Hüll hop research centre in Bavaria in 2012, in the same group of fruit forward varieties as Mandarina Bavaria and Huell Melon. Like them, it was bred for fruity aroma rather than classic noble spice.

Nothing about its aroma suggests a classic Hallertau. Instead of floral and spicy notes, it gives white grape, gooseberry and a little passion fruit and lemongrass. Many brewers compare it with a dry white wine, especially a Sauvignon Blanc. Alpha acid is moderate to high for an aroma hop, usually around 9 to 12%, which matters for how you plan your bitterness.

Hop aroma comes from volatile oils. Boiling drives most of them off within minutes, so a 60 minute addition of Hallertau Blanc gives bitterness and very little of the wine character. Brewers who try it in the kettle and find it disappointing have usually put it in too early.

The character survives best in three places: a short late boil addition of five minutes or less, a whirlpool held around 75 to 80 °C and the dry hop. Of those, the dry hop gives the clearest white wine note. A sensible starting point in a pale ale is around 3 to 4 g per litre, so 60 to 80 g in a 20 litre batch.

Because its alpha acid is fairly high, a big whirlpool addition of Hallertau Blanc adds more bitterness than people expect. Hot wort keeps isomerising alpha acids after the boil, more slowly but not at zero. A large whirlpool dose in a pale ale can add 10 IBU or more on its own, depending on how long the wort stays hot before you chill it.

The simplest approach is to bitter with a small 60 minute addition of a clean hop, keep the total calculated IBU modest and let Hallertau Blanc do its work late. If the beer comes out sharper than intended, trim the bittering charge next time rather than the aroma hop.

The white wine character fits beers with a light, dry base and not too much competition:

  • Pale ales and session IPAs on a pale malt base, where the gooseberry note stands out.
  • Belgian style blondes and saisons, where the hop's fruit meets a spicy, dry yeast character.
  • Wheat beers with a clean American wheat yeast rather than a clove heavy German one.
  • Hoppy lagers, where cold fermentation leaves the hop aroma very clear.

It is less convincing in a dark beer, where roast flavour buries it, or in a bitter, resinous IPA, where louder hops shout over it. If you want more fruit on top of the gooseberry, a small late addition of a citrus hop such as Amarillo adds orange without burying the wine note.
Catty notes and how to avoid them

Some tasters pick up a grassy or slightly catty edge in heavily dry hopped Hallertau Blanc beers, especially at high doses or with long contact time. That is common to several fruit hops of this kind. Keep dry hop contact to around three or four days at fermentation or cool temperatures, then move the beer off the hops.

Freshness matters too. Old hops kept warm develop cheesy and flat notes that no amount of dry hopping hides. In an Indian summer an opened foil can lose a lot of aroma in days if it sits out. Keep it frozen, sealed and away from the brewhouse until you are ready to add it.
Why one hop can taste so different

The same Hallertau Blanc can come across as gooseberry in one beer and plain grass in another. Yeast strain, fermentation temperature, timing of the dry hop and the oxygen picked up along the way all change what you taste. That is the chemistry of hop aroma at work. It is a big part of why brewers who understand it get more from every gram.

The white wine character reads best on a pale, dry base. Pale or Pilsner malt for 90% or more of the grist, a little wheat or oats for body and no more than about 5% light crystal malt is plenty. Darker caramel malts add toffee that clashes with gooseberry. Mash on the low side, around 64 to 66 °C, for a dry finish that lets the hop feel crisp rather than sweet.

Brew a simple pale ale at about 4.5% ABV on pale malt with a clean ale yeast. Bitter it to around 25 IBU with a neutral hop at 60 minutes. Then add 30 g of Hallertau Blanc in the whirlpool and 60 g as a dry hop. Pour it next to a glass of dry white wine, if you drink wine. See how much of the comparison holds.
faqs: What does Hallertau Blanc taste like?
White grape, gooseberry and a little passion fruit and lemongrass. Many brewers compare it with a dry white wine.
When should I add Hallertau Blanc?
Late: a short late boil addition, the whirlpool or the dry hop. A 60 minute addition loses most of its aroma.
Is Hallertau Blanc similar to Nelson Sauvin?
Both are often described with white wine terms, but they are different hops. Hallertau Blanc is generally lighter and leans more towards gooseberry and grape.
